expectedText:
JURY DUTY AND WITNESS LEAVE — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme Innovations LLC

JURY DUTY / WITNESS LEAVE NOTICE
Jordan Lee provides this notice to Acme Innovations LLC of time off requested under California law, for the reason checked below.

☐ Jury duty — service on an inquest jury or trial jury as required by law, before Superior Court of California, County of Sacramento.
☐ Witness appearance — required by subpoena or other court order to appear as a witness in a judicial proceeding before Superior Court of California, County of Sacramento.

Case number or matter reference, if known: _______________________________________________
Dates of service requested: September 8, 2026 through September 12, 2026
Date this notice is given to Acme Innovations LLC: _______________
Copy of jury summons, subpoena, or other court order: ☐ Attached ☐ To be provided when received

WHERE THIS PROTECTION IS CODIFIED TODAY
California's job protections for employees who take time off for jury duty or to appear in court as a witness were relocated out of the Labor Code and into the Fair Employment and Housing Act (FEHA), effective January 1, 2025. They are now codified at Government Code § 12945.8, most recently amended by AB 406 (Stats. 2025, Ch. 148), effective October 1, 2025, and are enforced by California's Civil Rights Department. Labor Code § 230 — which for many years contained these same jury-duty and witness-leave protections, and is still sometimes cited under that older number — remains on the books only in a transitional form: by its own terms it applies solely to alleged actions or inactions occurring on or before December 31, 2024, and it is scheduled to be repealed on January 1, 2035.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "(Amended by Stats. 2025, Ch. 148, Sec. 1.   (AB 406)   Effective October 1, 2025.)"
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.8 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.8, amendment history note (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12945.8)
  "(k) This section shall apply only to alleged actions or inactions occurring on or before December 31, 2024."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 230 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), Cal. Lab. Code § 230(k), transitional applicability limit (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=230.)
  "(l) This section shall remain in effect only until January 1, 2035, and as of that date is repealed."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 230 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), Cal. Lab. Code § 230(l), scheduled repeal date (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=230.)
  Known gap: This document treats Government Code § 12945.8, not Labor Code § 230, as the operative source of law for present-day jury-duty and witness-leave situations, because directly verifying the current statutory text — rather than assuming an older, frequently-cited Labor Code section still controls — showed the Legislature moved this protection. The Labor Code § 230(k) and § 230(l) citations below are two subsections of that same single Labor Code source, not independent sources of one another; the real independence in this clause is between the Government Code source and the Labor Code source, each fetched and confirmed identical twice, using two distinct User-Agent strings, directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov. This document does not independently verify secondary commentary (bill-tracking pages or law-firm summaries) about the legislative history of AB 2499 or AB 406; only the current statutory text itself, and Labor Code § 230's own applicability clause, were verified as primary sources.

JURY DUTY LEAVE PROTECTION
Under Government Code § 12945.8, an employer may not discharge an employee, or discriminate against an employee in any manner, for taking time off to serve as required by law on an inquest jury or trial jury. As a condition of taking that time off, the employee must give the employer reasonable advance notice of the employee's intention to take the time off, unless advance notice is not feasible.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "(1) Discharge or in any manner discriminate against an employee for taking time off to serve as required by law on an inquest jury or trial jury."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.8 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.8(a)(1), jury duty leave protection (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12945.8)
  "(c) (1) As a condition of taking time off for a purpose set forth in paragraph (1), (3), or (4) of subdivision (a), or subdivision (b), the employee shall give the employer reasonable advance notice of the employee’s intention to take time off, unless the advance notice is not feasible."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.8 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.8(c)(1), advance notice condition (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12945.8)
  Known gap: The jury-duty protection (subdivision (a)(1)) and its notice condition (subdivision (c)(1)) are two subsections of the same Government Code section, not independent sources of each other — both were confirmed against one fetched-and-verified copy of § 12945.8, checked twice with distinct User-Agent strings. This clause does not define how much notice counts as 'reasonable,' which the statute does not itself specify, and it does not restate the separate certification provisions in subdivision (c)(2)-(3) that can apply after an unscheduled absence, since this document did not resolve how those provisions interact with a jury summons an employee typically cannot schedule around.

WITNESS LEAVE PROTECTION (SUBPOENA OR COURT ORDER)
Under Government Code § 12945.8, an employer may not discharge an employee, or discriminate or retaliate against an employee in any manner, for taking time off to appear in court to comply with a subpoena or other court order as a witness in any judicial proceeding. This protection is expressly extended to, but is not limited to, an employee who is a victim — it is not a victim-only protection.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "(2) Discharge or in any manner discriminate or retaliate against an employee, including, but not limited to, an employee who is a victim, for taking time off to appear in court to comply with a subpoena or other court order as a witness in any judicial proceeding."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.8 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.8(a)(2), witness leave protection (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12945.8)
  "(c) (1) As a condition of taking time off for a purpose set forth in paragraph (1), (3), or (4) of subdivision (a), or subdivision (b), the employee shall give the employer reasonable advance notice of the employee’s intention to take time off, unless the advance notice is not feasible."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.8 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.8(c)(1), advance notice condition (paragraphs it covers) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12945.8)
  Known gap: This protection covers an employee compelled to appear as a witness by a subpoena or other court order; the verified text does not extend it to a voluntary or informal court appearance that isn't compelled that way. Unlike jury duty leave under paragraph (a)(1), the advance-notice condition in subdivision (c)(1) lists only paragraphs (1), (3), and (4) of subdivision (a), and subdivision (b), as subject to it — paragraph (a)(2), the witness-leave paragraph quoted here, is not among them. This document flags that omission as a deliberate reading of the statute's own enumeration, rather than assuming a notice requirement applies to witness leave by analogy to jury duty leave. Both citations below come from the same fetched-and-verified copy of § 12945.8, not from two independent sources.

PAY STATUS AND USE OF ACCRUED LEAVE
Government Code § 12945.8 does not itself require an employer to pay an employee's wages during jury duty or witness leave. Instead, the statute allows an employee to use vacation, personal leave, paid sick leave, or compensatory time off that is otherwise available to the employee under the employee's applicable terms of employment — unless a collective bargaining agreement provides otherwise — for time taken off for jury duty, witness leave, or the crime-victim leave purposes this same section separately addresses. The statute also states that it does not create a right to unpaid leave beyond, or in addition to, the 12 weeks of unpaid leave available under the federal Family and Medical Leave Act.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "(g) An employee may use vacation, personal leave, paid sick leave, or compensatory time off that is otherwise available to the employee under the applicable terms of employment, unless otherwise provided by a collective bargaining agreement, for time taken off for a purpose specified in subdivision (a) or (b). The entitlement of any employee under this section shall not be diminished by any collective bargaining agreement term or condition."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.8 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.8(g), use of accrued vacation, personal leave, paid sick leave, or compensatory time (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12945.8)
  "(h) This section does not create a right for an employee to take unpaid leave that exceeds the unpaid leave time allowed under, or is in addition to the unpaid leave time permitted by, the 12 weeks provided under the federal Family and Medical Leave Act of 1993 (29 U.S.C. Sec. 2601 et seq.)."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.8 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.8(h), no additional unpaid leave beyond the FMLA's 12 weeks (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12945.8)
  Known gap: This section does not create its own paid-leave benefit; whether time off is actually paid depends on whether the employee has, and chooses to use, other accrued paid leave, or on a separate employer policy or agreement this document doesn't address. This document does not independently verify other California statutes that address jury fees or per diem payments made to jurors by the court itself (as distinct from wages paid by the employer), which is a distinct topic from what this clause covers. Both citations below are subsections of the same fetched-and-verified copy of § 12945.8.

NO INTERFERENCE WITH LEAVE RIGHTS
It is an unlawful employment practice under Government Code § 12945.8 for an employer to interfere with, restrain, or deny the exercise of, or the attempt to exercise, any right this section provides — including the jury duty and witness leave rights described above.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "(f) It shall be an unlawful employment practice for an employer to interfere with, restrain, or deny the exercise of, or the attempt to exercise, any right provided under this section."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.8 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.8(f), prohibition on interference with section rights (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12945.8)
  Known gap: This section is part of the Fair Employment and Housing Act; this document does not detail FEHA's general administrative complaint and civil remedy process (filing with the Civil Rights Department, right-to-sue notices, and civil litigation under the surrounding FEHA statutes), because those general FEHA enforcement mechanics were not independently fetched and verified for this document. This is a deliberate correction against a natural assumption: the former Labor Code § 230 contained its own self-contained reinstatement-and-reimbursement remedy clause and its own misdemeanor penalty provision for willful refusal to rehire after a grievance determination, but the verified text of Government Code § 12945.8 fetched for this document contains neither a comparable self-contained remedy clause nor a misdemeanor provision — so this document does not assert that either exists in current law, only that interference with the section's rights is an unlawful employment practice, which the verified text does say.

RELATED BUT DISTINCT: CRIME-VICTIM AND DOMESTIC-VIOLENCE LEAVE
The same Government Code § 12945.8 that protects jury duty and witness leave also contains separate protections for an employee who is a victim of a qualifying act of violence, or who has a family member who is — covering time off to obtain a restraining order or other relief, time off to attend certain judicial proceedings related to the crime (a protection that, by the statute's own terms, commences January 1, 2026), and, for employers with 25 or more employees, a broader set of purposes such as relocating, seeking medical or psychological care, or arranging childcare because of the qualifying act of violence. This information sheet addresses only the jury-duty and witness-leave portions of this section.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "(4) Commencing January 1, 2026, discharge or in any manner discriminate or retaliate against an employee who is a victim or a family member of a victim for taking time off from work in order to attend judicial proceedings related to that crime, including, but not limited to, any delinquency proceeding, a postarrest release decision, plea, sentencing, postconviction release decision, or any proceeding where a right of that person is an issue."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.8 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.8(a)(4), crime-victim judicial-proceeding leave (commencing January 1, 2026) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12945.8)
  "(b) An employer with 25 or more employees shall not discharge or in any manner discriminate or retaliate against an employee who is a victim or who has a family member who is a victim for taking time off from work for any of the following purposes:"
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.8 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.8(b), broader victim/family-member leave for employers with 25 or more employees (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12945.8)
  Known gap: These crime-victim and domestic-violence leave protections are a substantial, separately defined topic — with their own definitions of 'victim,' 'qualifying act of violence,' 'family member,' and 'designated person,' their own notice and certification rules, a reasonable-accommodation requirement, and employer-size-dependent leave caps — that this document does not attempt to cover; it is flagged here only so a reader who came looking for the older, separately-known 'domestic violence leave' or Labor Code § 230.1 topic knows where that subject now lives. This document did not independently fetch or verify the current status of former Labor Code § 230.1, so it makes no claim about that section specifically.

Date: September 2, 2026
